periods.activity_title: Building Equilateral Triangles with Compass and Ruler

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

time_bands.activity: Begin by asking students to try drawing an equilateral triangle using only a marked ruler, inviting them to notice how much trial-and-error is involved. Establish that the arc method — locating a point equidistant from two given endpoints — gives a reliable, exact construction. Demonstrate drawing a 4 cm base AB on the board.

Students work through Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler...."). For each sub-part, they draw the base, swing two arcs of the given radius from each base endpoint, mark the intersection as the third vertex, and join. Circulate and prompt: 'Why are both arcs the same radius in the equilateral case?'

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles...."). They use the radius property — all points on a circle are equidistant from the centre — to justify why the resulting triangles are isosceles. Pairs compare constructions and explain the reasoning to each other.

Draw the class together to share observations: what made the arc intersection method trustworthy? Students articulate, in their own words, why C lies on both arcs and therefore AC = BC = 4 cm. Collect any remaining questions before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who swing arcs of unequal radii in parts (a)–(d) of the Construct exercise — a common slip when the triangle is not equilateral. The arc intersection explained through the 'equidistant point' idea from Grade 6 is the key conceptual anchor for everything that follows in this chapter. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150 (equal circles with centres A, B, C forming triangles) can serve as a self-study extension for students who complete the main tasks comfortably.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: When Do Three Lengths Make a Triangle? Discovering the Inequality

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151
textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
homework.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: if someone gives you three lengths, can you always build a triangle? Students attempt Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ("Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm....") in pairs, trying the arc method from section 7.1. They observe that the arcs fail to intersect and record what happens.

Groups share their impossible cases and search for more examples, recording each as a table of three lengths plus 'triangle or not'. Guide them toward the tent-tree-pole metaphor: the direct path (one side) is always shorter than a roundabout path via a third point (the other two sides combined). Students articulate their conjecture: any one side must be less than the sum of the other two.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ("Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality."). They check: is 8 < 3 + 4? Is 6 < 2 + 3? They write brief justifications without drawing, practising using the inequality as a decision rule.

Whole-class discussion: the triangle inequality as both necessary (no triangle when it fails) and sufficient (triangle exists when it holds). Students state the rule in their own words and give one self-invented example of each case — possible and impossible.

periods.teacher_notes: A common reasoning error is to check only one comparison (e.g., only the longest side against the sum of the other two) — prompt students to notice that for valid triangles the two shorter sides automatically satisfy their comparisons, so in practice only the longest-side check is critical, but the principle applies to all three pairs. The circle-intersection cases (circles touching, not intersecting, intersecting internally) presented in the textbook's visual proof provide a strong verification of the inequality as a geometric fact worth discussing if time permits.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: Applying the Triangle Inequality: Sorting and Finding Valid Third Sides

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159
homework.description: Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students work independently through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5...."). For each set, they identify the longest side, check whether it is less than the sum of the other two, and write a one-sentence justification. No construction is required — the inequality is the sole decision tool.

Groups tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 ("Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100...."), then move to Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 ("For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side...."). For the open-ended third-side task, they express the valid range as an inequality and look for a pattern in how the range bounds relate to the two given sides.

Groups share the range they found for each pair in Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 and the class formulates a general rule: if two sides are a and b, the third side x must satisfy |a − b| < x < a + b. Students test their rule against the cases in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156.

Quick consolidation: each student writes one valid and one invalid third-side value for two sides of their own choice and swaps with a partner to check. This quick peer-check cements the procedural fluency with the inequality.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly think only of the upper bound (third side < sum) and miss the lower bound (third side > difference); draw attention to the case 1, 100 in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 where the lower bound is most visible. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 (equilateral triangle of any sidelength) is assigned as homework to extend the reasoning about equilateral triangles built on the triangle inequality, connecting back to the equilateral-triangle construction established in section 7.1.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Angle Sum of a Triangle: Parallel-Line Proof and Angle Conditions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164
textbook_items_in_class.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°? If two angles are 70°, what is the third? If all angles are equal, what must each be?

homework.description: In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164 ("Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third....") by measuring angles in a few drawn triangles and summing them. They record results in a two-column table (pair of angles / third angle) and conjecture that the three angles always sum to 180°.

Walk through the formal parallel-line proof: draw XY through A parallel to BC, identify ∠XAB as an alternate interior angle equal to ∠B, and ∠YAC as an alternate interior angle equal to ∠C. The three angles at A (∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC) form a straight angle, so ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Students annotate a diagram in their notebooks with each reasoning step labeled.

Students apply the angle-sum property in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ("Find the third angle using a parallel-line argument when two angles are....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165 ("Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°?...."). For each, they first state whether the given pair allows a valid third angle and then compute it.

Class discussion: what happens when two given angles already sum to 180° or more? Students articulate the existence condition for a triangle given two angles: their sum must be strictly less than 180°. Pairs share one example each of a valid and an invalid pair.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is treating the angle-sum property as something to be memorised rather than derived; insisting that students trace back each labeled angle to the alternate-angle step keeps the deductive chain visible. Having established that ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°, the exterior-angle result (exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles) follows immediately and can be previewed here as a natural corollary — the formal treatment appears in section 7.3 p.166.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Constructing Triangles: SAS and ASA Cases

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

time_bands.activity: Briefly establish the SAS construction protocol: (1) draw the base, (2) construct the given angle at one endpoint using a protractor, (3) mark the second side length along the angle arm, (4) join to the other base endpoint. Students note the four steps before starting.

Students construct the three triangles in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ("Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm...."). For sub-part (c) with the 120° angle, circulate and prompt: is this still a valid triangle? (Yes — the included angle constraint only fails at or above 180°.)

Students move to Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ("Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°...."). They draw the base, construct each base angle, and mark the intersection of the two angle arms as vertex C. Sub-part (c) — 120° + 30° — prompts a check: is the angle sum less than 180°? Students note what happens when the two base angles are supplementary.

Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side?...."). Students find and share examples where the arm lines are parallel (sum = 180°) or point away from each other (sum > 180°). Class articulates the existence condition: sum of the two given angles must be strictly less than 180°.

periods.teacher_notes: In the ASA construction, students often place both angles at the same base endpoint rather than one at each end — a quick diagram on the board showing the two arms meeting at C prevents this. Having established through the angle-sum property that the two given angles must sum to less than 180°, students can check existence before lifting their compasses, turning construction into a planned rather than trial-and-error activity.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Exterior Angles and Angle Conditions: Reasoning from the Angle-Sum Property

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not. Find the third angle in each valid case.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166
textbook_items_in_class.description: Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163 ("For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not...."). They apply the angle-sum condition: the chosen second angle must be strictly less than 180° minus the given angle. For each valid pair, they compute the third angle.

Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163 ("Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°...."). Students check each pair's sum: if it equals or exceeds 180°, no triangle is possible. They write a one-sentence deductive justification for each case, using the angle-sum property as the warrant.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values...."). They compute several cases, record exterior angle and the pair of non-adjacent interior angles, and derive the exterior-angle theorem: exterior angle = sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles. This follows deductively from the angle-sum property and the linear-pair property.

Students state the exterior-angle theorem in their own words and verify it with one self-chosen triangle. A volunteer explains the two-step deductive chain: (1) angle sum = 180°; (2) exterior angle + adjacent interior angle = 180°; therefore exterior angle = sum of the other two.

periods.teacher_notes: A typical error is computing the exterior angle as 180° minus just one interior angle (the adjacent one) rather than the sum of the two non-adjacent ones; asking students to label the adjacent and non-adjacent angles before computing prevents this confusion. The derivation of the exterior-angle theorem as a direct consequence of the parallel-line angle-sum proof reinforces the deductive structure that runs through section 7.3.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Folding and Drawing Altitudes: Perpendicular Distance from a Vertex

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity, section 7.4 p.168
textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168
textbook_items_in_class.description: Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts out a triangle from paper and completes Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ("Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base."). They fold so the two halves of the base coincide, crease sharply, and check with a protractor that the crease meets the base at 90°. Brief pair discussion: why does folding create a perpendicular crease?

Students tackle Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ("Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?"). They sketch a right-angled triangle and identify the two legs as altitudes of the right-angle vertex, confirming perpendicularity. Class shares and names the type: right-angled triangle.

Students use ruler and set square to construct the altitude in Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ("Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square...."). They align the ruler along BC, place the set square on the ruler, slide until the vertical edge touches A, and draw. For the extended-base case, the base line is extended before applying the set square. Students annotate the right-angle symbol at the foot of the altitude.

Students compare their paper-folded altitude with their set-square-drawn altitude on the same triangle. They articulate that both methods produce the same perpendicular segment, reinforcing the definition: the altitude from a vertex is the perpendicular distance from that vertex to the opposite side (or its extension).

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the altitude with the median — a brief contrast (altitude is perpendicular, median goes to the midpoint) at the start helps. In the extended-base case of Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169, some students forget to extend the base before placing the set square; demonstrate this sub-step explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Triangles by Sides and Angles: Building the Complete Map

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

homework.description: Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? (Note: other measurements can take any values.)

time_bands.activity: Introduce the two classification axes through student input: classify by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse). Students fill in a two-axis grid in their notebooks with the six types and one example sketch each, drawing on constructions from earlier units of this chapter as source material.

Students construct Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY."). After each construction, they name the triangle by both sides and angles on their diagram.

Groups tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle."). For each combination, they attempt a construction or use the angle-sum property to argue why it is impossible.

Class shares findings from Figure it Out Q4: (a) and (b) are impossible because an equilateral triangle has all angles 60° — acute; (c) and (d) are possible because isosceles triangles allow varied angles. Students update their two-axis grid to mark which combinations are impossible.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume that 'isosceles' and 'equilateral' are mutually exclusive — point out that an equilateral triangle satisfies the definition of isosceles (at least two equal sides) and can be considered a special case. The angle-sum property established in section 7.3 is the key tool for ruling out combinations such as right-angled or obtuse-angled equilateral triangles.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: Circle Intersections and Constructing Triangles from Three Sides

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158 ("Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle."). They draw circles of the given arc radii from the two base endpoints and observe whether the circles touch at exactly one point or fail to meet, recording the sidelengths and the geometric outcome.

Groups compare their examples and identify the boundary condition: circles touch when the third side equals exactly the sum (or the absolute difference) of the other two. From the three circle-intersection cases (intersect, touch, separate), they collectively frame a complete existence-checking procedure in ordered steps.

Students take up Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 ("For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'?...."). They test several sets and reason: the two shorter sides are each trivially less than the sum of the remaining two (since the remaining two include the longest side), so only the comparison involving the longest side is ever critical.

Whole-class consolidation: students state the complete decision procedure in their own words — identify the longest side, check whether it is strictly less than the sum of the other two — and confirm that this single check is both necessary and sufficient.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the triangle inequality from a rule to a geometric fact grounded in circle intersection; watch for students who treat the boundary (touching circles) as a valid triangle case — a degenerate triangle with zero area is a useful concept to name here. Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 surfaces an elegant efficiency result: when three lengths are given, only the largest need be tested, which saves time in Figure it Out exercises throughout the chapter.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Putting SAS and ASA to Work: Extended Construction Practice

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.

time_bands.activity: Students engage with Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 ("Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...."). They test increasingly large angles (90°, 135°, 179°) as the included angle between two sides of fixed length and record whether a triangle results. They reason: as long as the included angle is less than 180°, the two arms meet at a distinct third vertex.

Students construct all three cases in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ("Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm....") using the four-step SAS protocol. They measure the third side in each completed triangle and note how it changes with the included angle.

Students construct the three ASA cases in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ("Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°...."). Before each construction, they check the angle-sum condition. Sub-part (c) — 120° + 30° = 150° < 180° — proceeds; students note that the resulting triangle has a 30° angle at C.

Pairs compare their completed constructions and identify which given information (SAS vs ASA) led to a unique triangle and whether any case yielded more than one possible shape. Class discussion surfaces that SAS and ASA each produce a unique triangle (given the information holds the existence condition).

periods.teacher_notes: Students who completed Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 in an earlier unit may work more quickly here; use the extra time to ask them to measure the third side in each completed SAS triangle and compare — this foreshadows congruence conditions without naming them. A common construction slip in the ASA case is drawing both angle arms from the same vertex; a quick labelling step (mark L and R base vertices before picking up the protractor) prevents this.

periods.activity_title: Shortest Path on a Box: Applying Triangle Geometry to a Spatial Puzzle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates. (Hint diagram shows unfolded surfaces.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? (Note: other measurements can take any values.)

time_bands.activity: Introduce Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172 ("Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk on the surfaces to the opposite corner...."). Students examine the hint diagram showing unfolded surfaces and identify that 'walking on surfaces' becomes 'walking on the flat unfolded net' — the shortest path on the flat net is a straight line.

Groups unfold a small cardboard box (or draw the net on paper), mark the spider's start and end corners, and draw a straight line across the net. They measure this straight-line distance and compare it with the path that goes over one face only. Groups try at least two different unfoldings (over top, over side) to see which yields the shorter straight-line distance, recording each path length.

Students attempt Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements?...."). They experiment with different values of AB (as long as AB < 5 cm, the hypotenuse constraint is satisfied) and construct several right-angled triangles, discovering that infinitely many such triangles exist — the hypotenuse and the right angle together underdetermine the triangle.

Class discussion connects both tasks: the straight-line path on the unfolded net is the shortest because any other surface path, when unfolded, would be a bent path — longer by the triangle inequality. Students articulate the connection between the triangle inequality and the shortest-path result in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The shortest-path-on-a-box task is genuinely open: different unfolding strategies yield different candidate paths, and the shortest is not obvious in advance — encourage groups to compare rather than compete. For Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170, students who think a right angle plus a hypotenuse uniquely determines the triangle need a counterexample; constructing two or three instances with different base lengths quickly dispels this.
materials: small cardboard box or printed net

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: From Existence to Construction to Classification

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156

textbook_items_in_class.description: Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

time_bands.activity: Open with a rapid oral survey connecting the chapter's three big ideas: (1) the arc-intersection method for constructing triangles from given measurements (sections 7.1–7.3); (2) the triangle inequality as the existence condition for three-side construction, and the angle-sum property (∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°) as the existence condition for angle-based construction (sections 7.2–7.3); (3) altitude as perpendicular distance and the two classification systems by sides and angles (sections 7.4–7.5). Students contribute one fact each to a collective mind-map on the board.

Students revisit Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain....") as a rapid classification warm-up, then move to Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle...."). The key argument — that equilateral triangles have three 60° angles and cannot accommodate a right or obtuse angle — connects the angle-sum property to the classification of triangle types.

Groups work on Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°....") as a synthesis item that chains: construct the triangle (SAS or SSS), apply the angle-sum property to find the third interior angle, and then apply the exterior-angle theorem. Students write out each logical step before computing, making the deductive chain explicit.

Students write a three-sentence summary in their own words: (1) how to decide whether three measurements can form a triangle; (2) the relationship that holds among any triangle's angles; (3) how altitude and triangle type are connected. Volunteers share and the class refines phrasing. This closing consolidation ensures that the chapter's core ideas — triangle inequality, angle-sum property, and altitude-based classification — are stated in the students' own register.

periods.teacher_notes: Because this unit synthesises the entire chapter, it can draw on any of the constructions and results by name — the arc-intersection method, the triangle inequality, the parallel-line angle-sum proof, the exterior-angle theorem, the altitude-as-perpendicular definition, and the six triangle types — without specifying which earlier unit introduced each. A common persistent confusion to surface and resolve here is the mistaken belief that equilateral triangles are not isosceles; the angle-sum argument shows all three angles must be 60° (acute), ruling out right and obtuse combinations cleanly.

items.prompt: A triangle has all three sides of different lengths and all three angles less than 90°. Which pair of terms correctly classifies this triangle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — Scalene and acute-angled. All three sides are different (scalene), and all angles are less than 90° (acute-angled).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-axis classification: by sides (equilateral / isosceles / scalene) and by angles (acute / right / obtuse).

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly applies both classification axes simultaneously.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses 'all sides different' with 'two sides equal'; knows the angle classification correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies the side classification but misremembers that all angles less than 90° makes a triangle acute, not right-angled.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses equilateral (all sides equal) with scalene (all sides different); equilateral also implies acute, so the angle part is accidentally correct.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the two-column classification grid (by sides and by angles) in your notebook and apply each definition to the given triangle one axis at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: Give your own example of a triangle that is both isosceles and obtuse-angled, and explain why an equilateral triangle can never be obtuse-angled.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Kiran claims that three lengths of 4 cm, 6 cm, and 11 cm can form a triangle. Explain clearly why Kiran is wrong, using the triangle inequality.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The triangle inequality requires each side to be less than the sum of the other two. Check the longest side: 11 cm must be less than 4 + 6 = 10 cm. Since 11 > 10, the inequality fails and no triangle can be formed. Kiran is wrong.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the longest side and check whether it is strictly less than the sum of the other two, using the triangle inequality as the existence condition.

inclusivity.support: Talk through the three lengths with a partner: point to the longest one and ask whether you can add the remaining two to beat it.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the value 11 to the largest whole-number length that would make a triangle possible, and justify your choice.

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle PQR, ∠P = 48° and ∠Q = 57°. Using the angle-sum property, find ∠R and explain each step of your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angle-sum property states that the three interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°. So ∠P + ∠Q + ∠R = 180°. Substituting: 48° + 57° + ∠R = 180°, giving 105° + ∠R = 180°, so ∠R = 75°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property (∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°) and subtract the two known angles from 180°.

inclusivity.support: Before writing, discuss with a partner: if the three angles must add up to 180°, and two of them together give 105°, what must the third be?
inclusivity.challenge: If ∠P and ∠Q were both increased by 10°, what would ∠R become, and what type of triangle (by angles) would result?

exercise.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Priya wants to construct a triangle given two angles of 95° and 90° and the side between them. Explain, with a clear argument, whether this construction will succeed or fail.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two given angles sum to 95° + 90° = 185°, which exceeds 180°. By the angle-sum property, the three interior angles of any triangle must sum to exactly 180°. If two angles already exceed 180°, there is no positive value left for the third angle — it would have to be negative, which is impossible. Therefore the construction fails; no triangle exists with these two angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the sum of the two given angles is less than 180°, using the angle-sum property as the existence condition for the ASA construction.

inclusivity.support: First add the two given angles together, then ask: is there any positive number of degrees left for the third angle if the total must be 180°?
inclusivity.challenge: Find the largest whole-number value for the second angle (keeping the first at 95°) for which the construction would succeed, and identify the type of triangle that would result.

items.prompt: Using compass and ruler, describe the exact steps to construct an equilateral triangle with side length 5 cm. Then state the length of each side of the completed triangle and give one reason why the construction guarantees all three sides are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Steps: (1) Draw segment AB = 5 cm. (2) With centre A and radius 5 cm, swing an arc above AB. (3) With centre B and radius 5 cm, swing a second arc to intersect the first; label the intersection C. (4) Draw AC and BC. All three sides are 5 cm. The guarantee: C lies on the arc centred at A (so AC = 5 cm) and also on the arc centred at B (so BC = 5 cm); AB was drawn as 5 cm; therefore AB = AC = BC = 5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-arc intersection method: a point at the intersection of arcs of equal radius from both base endpoints is equidistant from both endpoints.

inclusivity.support: Draw the base segment first, then use your compass opened to the same width as the base to swing both arcs — the setting must not change between the two arcs.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend the construction: using the same equilateral triangle as a base, construct a second equilateral triangle on one of its sides to form a rhombus, and name the angles of the rhombus.

exercise.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: A student is given three sticks of lengths 7 cm, 9 cm, and 14 cm. (a) Check using the triangle inequality whether these lengths can form a triangle. (b) If the longest stick were replaced by one of length 17 cm (with the other two unchanged), would a triangle still be possible? Show your working for both parts.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Longest side = 14 cm. Check: 14 < 7 + 9 = 16. Since 14 < 16, the inequality holds. A triangle is possible. (b) Longest side = 17 cm. Check: 17 < 7 + 9 = 16. Since 17 > 16, the inequality fails. No triangle is possible with lengths 7, 9, 17 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the longest side and check whether it is strictly less than the sum of the remaining two sides.

inclusivity.support: Write the three lengths in order from smallest to largest, then add the two smaller ones and compare the total with the largest.
inclusivity.challenge: Find all whole-number lengths x (in cm) that could replace the 14 cm stick so that a triangle with sides 7, 9, and x is possible, and express the answer as an inequality.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Triangle LMN has ∠L = 65° and LM = 5 cm, LN = 7 cm. (a) Name the construction case (SAS or ASA) and write the four construction steps in order. (b) Using the angle-sum property, find ∠M + ∠N without measuring, given that ∠L = 65°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) This is the SAS (two sides and included angle) case. Steps: 1. Draw segment LM = 5 cm. 2. At L, construct an angle of 65° using a protractor and draw the angle arm. 3. Mark N on the angle arm at distance 7 cm from L. 4. Join M to N to complete triangle LMN. (b) By the angle-sum property, ∠L + ∠M + ∠N = 180°. So ∠M + ∠N = 180° − 65° = 115°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the SAS configuration (two sides and their included angle), follow the four-step construction protocol, then apply the angle-sum property to find the remaining angle total.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the triangle roughly first and label which angle is between the two given sides — that is the included angle, and the construction always begins with the side opposite the unknown vertex.
inclusivity.challenge: If ∠M = ∠N, use part (b) to find the exact measure of each, and name the type of triangle LMN is by both sides and angles.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: In triangle ABC, ∠B = 90°. Which of the following statements about the altitudes of this triangle is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Side AB is an altitude from A to AC.

options.label: B
options.text: Side BC is an altitude from C to AB.

options.label: C
options.text: Side AB is an altitude from B to AC, and side BC is an altitude from B to AC.

options.label: D
options.text: Side AB is an altitude from A to BC, and side BC is an altitude from C to AB.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: D — In a right-angled triangle, the two legs meeting at the right angle are each perpendicular to the other; AB ⊥ BC, so AB is the altitude from A to the line BC, and BC is the altitude from C to the line AB.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition of altitude (perpendicular segment from a vertex to the opposite side) and use the right angle at B to identify which sides serve as altitudes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the foot of the altitude (which must lie on the opposite side) with the vertex; AB runs from A to B, not to AC.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student identifies the correct pair of sides but misidentifies the vertex the altitude drops from; BC runs from B to C, making it an altitude from C to AB or from B to AC, but not both simultaneously in the same description.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies both legs but confuses the foot of each altitude; both altitudes cannot drop to AC — they drop to the other leg.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly applies the definition: AB ⊥ BC means AB is the altitude from A to side BC, and BC is the altitude from C to side AB.

inclusivity.support: Draw a right-angled triangle and mark the right angle; the altitude from a vertex must land on the opposite side at a right angle — trace each leg and check which side it lands on perpendicularly.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain why a right-angled triangle has exactly two sides that are also altitudes, and describe what the third altitude (from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse) looks like.

exercise.description: Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Two circles are drawn: one with centre P and radius 5 cm, and another with centre Q where PQ = 8 cm and the second circle has radius 4 cm. (a) Do the two circles intersect, touch at one point, or not intersect? Show the calculation. (b) What does this geometric outcome tell you about whether a triangle with sides 5 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm can be constructed?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The circles intersect when the distance between centres (8 cm) is less than the sum of the radii (5 + 4 = 9 cm) and greater than the absolute difference (|5 − 4| = 1 cm). Since 1 < 8 < 9, the circles intersect at two points. (b) The two intersection points each give a valid third vertex C of a triangle with sides PC = 5 cm, QC = 4 cm, and PQ = 8 cm. So a triangle with sides 5 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm can be constructed. This also follows directly from the triangle inequality: 8 < 5 + 4 = 9 ✓.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the distance between centres with the sum and absolute difference of the radii to determine the circle-intersection case, then link the outcome to the triangle inequality.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the two circles approximately; mark PQ = 8 cm as the distance between centres, then ask: is 8 less than 5 + 4? That single comparison tells you whether the circles overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the range of valid distances PQ (keeping the two radii fixed at 5 cm and 4 cm) for which the circles intersect at two points, and express it as a double inequality.

exercise.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle XYZ, an exterior angle at Z measures 130°. If ∠X = 55°, find ∠Y using the exterior-angle theorem. Verify your answer using the angle-sum property.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: By the exterior-angle theorem, the exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles: exterior ∠Z = ∠X + ∠Y. So 130° = 55° + ∠Y, giving ∠Y = 75°. Verification using the angle-sum property: the interior angle at Z = 180° − 130° = 50°. Then ∠X + ∠Y + ∠Z = 55° + 75° + 50° = 180° ✓.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the exterior-angle theorem (exterior angle = sum of two non-adjacent interior angles) then verify with the angle-sum property.

inclusivity.support: Label which two interior angles are 'non-adjacent' to the exterior angle at Z — they are the angles at the other two vertices — then use the exterior-angle relationship to find the missing one.
inclusivity.challenge: Change ∠X to 70° and the exterior angle at Z to 130°; show that no valid triangle exists and explain why using both the exterior-angle theorem and the angle-sum property.

exercise.description: Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

items.prompt: A path on the surface of a rectangular box runs from one corner to the opposite corner by crossing exactly two faces. The box measures 6 cm long, 4 cm wide, and 3 cm tall. If the path crosses the top face and one long side, what is the straight-line distance of this path on the unfolded net? Show your calculation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Unfolding the top face and the long side together gives a flat rectangle. The path starts at one corner of the top face and ends at the diagonally opposite corner of the long side. On the unfolded net, the horizontal distance is (length of top face) + (height of box) = 6 + 3 = 9 cm, and the vertical distance is the width = 4 cm. The straight-line distance = √(9² + 4²) = √(81 + 16) = √97 ≈ 9.85 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Unfold the two faces into a flat rectangle; the shortest surface path becomes the straight-line diagonal of the resulting rectangle, computed using the Pythagorean relationship (right-angled triangle).

inclusivity.support: Draw or fold a paper net of the two faces side by side; mark the start and end corners on the flat net and draw the straight line between them, then measure or calculate its length.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the straight-line distance if the path instead crosses the top face and one short end face, and determine which of the two unfolding strategies gives the shorter path.

exercise.description: Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates. (Hint diagram shows unfolded surfaces.)

items.prompt: Ravi says: 'I can draw a triangle that is both equilateral and right-angled.' Anika says: 'I can draw a triangle that is both isosceles and obtuse-angled.' Using the angle-sum property and the definitions of triangle types, show which claim is correct and which is impossible.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ravi's claim (equilateral and right-angled): An equilateral triangle has all three angles equal. By the angle-sum property, 3 × ∠A = 180°, so each angle = 60°. A right-angled triangle must have one angle = 90°. Since 60° ≠ 90°, no equilateral triangle can be right-angled. Ravi's claim is impossible. Anika's claim (isosceles and obtuse-angled): An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Let the two equal base angles each be 40° and the vertex angle be 180° − 80° = 100°. Since 100° > 90°, the triangle is obtuse-angled. Anika's claim is correct; an example is a triangle with angles 40°, 40°, 100°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property to the equilateral case to show all angles must be 60° (ruling out 90°); then construct a valid isosceles example with an obtuse vertex angle.

inclusivity.support: For each claim, write the angle-sum equation first and substitute what you know about each type — let the equations show you whether the combination is possible.
inclusivity.challenge: Find all possible values of the obtuse angle in an isosceles obtuse-angled triangle and express the range as an inequality.
